Michigan coach Kyle Whittingham fires embattled offensive coordinator Jason Beck
articles.content: ANN ARBOR (AP) — Kyle Whittingham has made his first major move as Michigan’s coach, firing embattled offensive coordinator Jason Beck. “The results have not matched our desired outcome, and I felt that a change in leadership was required for our offense,” Whittingham said in a statement Sunday night. “We need to put our offensive players and the entire team in the best possible position to be successful.” Whittingham said after watching film of a 15-6 loss to rival Michigan State, he knew it was time to fire offensive coordinator Jason Beck. “It became apparent to me that we needed to make the change now,” Whittingham said Monday, a day after making the move. Whittingham insisted there was “zero” outside influence in the decision. Whittingham named Jim Harding as interim offensive coordinator for the rest of the season. Harding is the team’s offensive line coach and assistant head coach. He worked with Whittingham for 12 seasons at Utah, including two years as co-offensive coordinator. The Wolverines (5-4, 2-4 Big Ten) started the season ranked No. 16 in the AP Top 25 and have fallen short of expectations with one of the nation’s worst offenses, shaky special teams and a defense that has been solid at times. Michigan might fall short of earning a bowl bid as underdogs at No. 18 Oregon (6-3, 3-2) on Saturday, at home against No. 4 UCLA and against rival and 21st-ranked Ohio State on the road. The Wolverines barely avoided being shut out for the first time since 2014 against rival Michigan State, scoring with 1:35 left in a 15-6 loss after being favored to win by two touchdowns. Michigan was been held scoreless in the first half three times in a season for the first time since 1979. Under Beck, the Wolverines were ranked No. 132 out of 138 FBS teams in total offense, No. 126 in scoring, No. 125 in passing offense and No. 109 in rushing offense. Beck was Whittingham’s offensive coordinator at Utah last season, helping the team rank No. 2 in rushing, No. 4 in total offense and No. 5 in scoring offense. He was New Mexico’s offensive coordinator in 2024. “We appreciate the hard work and effort that Jason has dedicated to the program,” Whittingham said. “Jason is a great man and coach, and unfortunately, it did not work out the way that we wanted it to at Michigan. We wish Jason and his family nothing but the best in the future.” After a 20-14 loss to Minnesota last month, when quarterback Bryce Underwood did not play well one week after making many positive plays in a loss to Iowa, tight end Zach Marshall criticized Beck in group text messages that were leaked on social media. Marshall publicly apologized, but he did not play in the following game against Penn State due to a noninjury situation, according to Whittingham. Michigan’s quarterback situation that Beck managed was closely watched with a former No. 1 recruit getting benched in favor of a backup with a familiar name. Underwood was taken out of the game against Penn State after the team was held scoreless in a first half for the first of three straight home games. Tommy Carr, whose grandfathers are College Hall of Famers and brother is Notre Dame’s quarterback, successfully filled in for Underwood in a comeback win against the Nittany Lions. Carr struggled against the Spartans, but Whittingham said the offensive coaches wanted to stick with him and the head coach said he agreed with their call. No matter who has taken snaps this season, Michigan has failed to consistently make plays on offense and it cost Beck his job.

Traverse City Coast Guard helicopter rescues sailor off Wisconsin
articles.content: The U.S. Coast Guard said a helicopter crew based in Traverse City helped rescue a man whose sailboat became stranded on Green Bay island southeast of Menominee, Michigan, at about 8 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 7. The Coast Guard said the man, who was not identified in a release, was rescued by the helicopter crew and was transported to Menominee Regional Airport, where he then was transferred to emergency medical services for treatment of hypothermia. “This rescue reflects the coordination and professionalism of our Coast Guard crews and watchstanders,” said Gregory Grubbs, command duty officer of the Coast Guard Great Lakes District Command Center. “As conditions on the Great Lakes become increasingly unpredictable this time of year, we remind boaters to check weather forecasts before getting underway, ensure their vessels and safety equipment are in working order, and always have a reliable means of communicating in an emergency. The man radioed a mayday call at about 6:08 p.m. Saturday after his 28-foot sailboat lost power. The man reported high winds and concerns that his vessel could capsize. The sailboat became disabled after its battery died approximately 11 miles northwest of the Sturgeon Bay Canal in Wisconsin, the Coast Guard said. The Coast Guard directed a 45-foot Response Boat-Medium crew from Coast Guard Station Sturgeon Bay to respond, and issued an urgent marine information broadcast due to the man’s inability to anchor and difficulties maintaining communications. An MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew from Coast Guard Air Station Traverse City also responded. While awaiting assistance, the man reported that his sailboat had capsized, but he was able to right it before it ran aground on a sandbar. Both Coast Guard crews arrived on scene at approximately 8 p.m. Shallow water prevented the boat crew from reaching the sailboat. The helicopter crew lowered a rescue swimmer to assist the man before hoisting him aboard the helicopter The Coast Guard said there were no signs of pollution from the grounded sailboat.

Apps to distract you from the endless cycle of doomscrolling
articles.description: It's hard to break the cycle of doomscrolling, but there are plenty of apps that can help you spend more time on content that’s engaging and productive.
articles.content: You open your phone to check the time or a quick message. The next thing you know, an hour has passed and you’ve scrolled through endless celebrity drama, cat videos, awful news stories, influencer rants, and whatever else the algorithm decided to throw at you. Even though you probably don’t want to keep wasting your time and energy on this mind-numbing content, you do it again the next day. Doomscrolling, the habit of spending excessive amounts of time consuming content on social media, has become incredibly widespread. A survey from last year found that 64% of Americans say they doomscroll. Researchers have warned that doomscrolling can negatively affect several aspects of your well-being, including your mental health and attention span. Spending long periods scrolling can lead to brain fatigue, difficulty focusing, and disrupted sleep. And if a lot of the content you’re consuming is negative or stressful, it can leave you feeling disheartened, anxious, and emotionally drained. It’s hard to break the cycle of doomscrolling, but there are plenty of apps that provide content that’s engaging and productive. Of course, you could always read a book or go for a walk (we have a guide on how to stop doomscrolling), but this list is for when you have a few spare minutes and want something to do on your phone that isn’t endless scrolling. Finch is a self-care pet app that’s designed to help you build healthy habits. You care for a cute virtual pet by completing small daily goals, such as drinking enough water, going on a walk, and practicing mindfulness. You can write about your day, complete a breathing exercise, or send good vibes to a friend by adding them to the app. The more self-care you do, the more your pet thrives. The app offers a fun way to trade mindless scrolling for small moments of self-care. Finch is available for free on iOS and Android. Libby is a free reading app that connects you to your local public library’s digital collection of ebooks, audiobooks, and magazines. All you need is a library card to borrow thousands of titles, which makes it easy to turn screen time into something productive. You can explore a new book during a commute or while waiting at a doctor’s office, turning moments when your fingers might otherwise itch to scroll into opportunities to read. Libby is available for free on iOS and Android. If you want to take a break from doomscrolling and try something creative, Dudel Draw might be a good app for you. Each day, the app gives you a random shape that you turn into a drawing. These daily shapes vary from basic geometrical forms to more complex and abstract designs. You can also get your friends in on the creativity with some fun competition by comparing your different creations, which could provide a nice break from sending each other endless TikToks or Instagram Reels. Dudel Draw is available for free on iOS. If you still want to feel connected to the world without scrolling through social media, you can check out Radio Garden. The app lets you listen to over 25,000 live radio stations from across the globe. Once you open the app, you’ll see green dots marking cities and towns. Tap any dot to listen to radio stations broadcasting from that location. You can add favorites or search for radio stations, countries, and places. Radio Garden is free, but it also offers an ad-free premium plan for $2.99 per month. The app is available on both iOS and Android. Elevate is an app designed to help improve focus, memory, reading, math skills, and other cognitive abilities. It includes over 40 games to train different abilities you use in everyday life, from reading faster to comparing prices more efficiently. You can track training streaks and compare your mind’s performance over time. The app offers a free version with access to three games per day, or a yearly subscription of $39.99 for unlimited access. It’s available on both iOS and Android. Vocabulary is an app that helps you learn new words every day. You can pick your difficulty level and choose categories that interest you, like emotions, the human body, business, and more. Each word comes with a definition, example sentences, and a guide on how to pronounce it. The app also includes mini-games to help you review the words you’ve learned. You can set a goal of how many words you want to learn each week and create a regular learning routine. Vocabulary offers a free trial, and then costs $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year. It’s available on iOS and Android. If you’re a geography nerd looking to test your knowledge or just want to improve your geography skills, Seterra is perfect for you. The app features over 300 different games to test your map skills. You can test your knowledge of world flags; discover oceans, seas, and rivers; and explore mountain ranges and volcanoes across the globe. Seterra lets you track your progress across categories and see leaderboards for top scorers for each game. The app is free and available on both iOS and Android. The NYT Games app offers several word, logic, and number games that change every day to exercise your mind. You can play the crossword, try the word-guessing game Wordle, group words with a common theme in Connections, see how many words you can make from seven letters in Spelling Bee, and more. The app costs $5.99 per month for unlimited access and archives, but some games like Wordle, Strands, and the Mini Crossword are available to play for free. NYT Games is available on both iOS and Android. If you want to learn a new language but want to try something other than Duolingo, Drops is a good option. The app uses visually engaging mini‑games to help you build vocabulary and common phrases in more than 45 languages, with bite‑sized lessons designed to be completed in about five minutes a day. Drops is designed for both beginners and experts who want to grow their foreign language vocabulary. The free version of the app offers five-minute lessons per day. You can get unlimited access and premium features for $11.99 per month or $79.99 per year. The app is available on both iOS and Android. articles.title: Zohran Mamdani has a mustache now. We cannot take this lightly | Dave Schilling
articles.content: The once-bearded New York mayor has downsized his facial hair. Does it work? I’ve battled with facial hair almost my entire adult life. I started growing it early, turning me into a pubescent villain from a spaghetti western. I was told by my parents not to shave it off, lest it grow back more furious than before. I just had to walk around high school looking like a hungover bond trader, which did nothing for my popularity. Once I hit proper adulthood, I grew a real beard, one that could effectively hide my chubby infant face. Now, I shave regularly, so that passersby don’t get a gander at my prodigious gray hair. Yes, my temples are whiter than the Lakers’ starting lineup, but a full-on Santa beard just exacerbates the problem. I am old, and getting older. I could follow the lead of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and grow a mustache instead. Mamdani rose to political prominence with a thick, black beard. The mustache is like Teddy Roosevelt shaving his own mustache off and settling for a soul patch. The beard made Mamdani’s already sunny face even more “cool dad” adjacent. It made him look both more rugged and somehow more approachable, like the most affable econ professor the East Village had ever known. But that nice guy beard is gone, replaced with a 70s-style mustache. I’ll be monitoring the situation for increased thickness, volume, and contour variation. Whenever a public figure changes their look, it’s a shock. A famous actor goes blonde and it’s headline news for the gossip industrial complex. A new piercing or a bit of plastic surgery can launch a thousand memes. But a mustache is another thing entirely. A mustache evokes a very particular reaction, considering its association with retired baseball players, sleazy used car dealers, and 20th-century union-busting oil barons. On a politician, it’s a bit undignified. Look, I’m no class traitor. I’m not fully anti-mustache. I believe in the working person’s right to a Tom Selleck special on their upper lip. My father, an air force master sergeant, had a mustache for most of the 1990s. When he left home to go fight in the Gulf war, he had the ‘stache. He came back with it, plus a Tabasco bottle filled with Kuwaiti sand. Mustaches are in my blood. They’re my birthright, but I can’t even begin to dream about a world where I have one. It runs counter to everything I believe myself to be – a man who can’t even figure out how to properly put air in my tires. I’ve tried to use a hammer on the wrong end more than once. I haven’t cleaned a single gutter in my entire life. For me, a mustache would be the lowest form of stolen valor. The only way I could be more disingenuous would be if I started dressing like Bruce Springsteen on the Born to Run cover. I grant Zohran his mustache, even if I see him on MS Now and think for a second that it’s Bob Hoskins in a toupee. Zohran’s mustache isn’t even the facial hair of the year – that title goes to Oliver Reed in the recently re-released 1971 film The Devils. But it has grown on me (pun intended), and I accept his decision to alter his personal brand ever so slightly. With that said, we must be steadfast in who we, as a culture, allow to wear a mustache. John Waters is grandfathered in, as the filth-monger director without his wispy facial hair would be as sacreligious as all of his movies. Timothée Chalamet grew a mustache for Marty Supreme, but if he wore that thing permanently, I’d have to send him a strongly worded letter. Barack Obama with a mustache would conjure images of the bartender from The Love Boat. We must hold the line. The mustache will always have blue-collar connotations. There are always outliers, but the vibe is the vibe. The mustache is powerful, it’s direct, and it is unequivocal. As a tool of personal identity, it might be unmatched. If you have one, you are guaranteed to be “the mustache guy” in your circle of friends. Some people might even keep your number in their phone as “Mr Mustache”. So, unless you can confidently go on Morning Joe and be called “Magnum PI”, then don’t do it. Don’t let GQ or some other style magazine pressure you into following the inevitable Mamdani-led trend. You are not him. You are not Jacob Elordi. Don’t make the decision lightly. Study, ponder, consult. Sure, you can shave off a mustache in a few minutes, but you can’t undo the damage to your social life if your facial hair flops. You must accept this. You have to embrace it, otherwise the mustache will consume you. This is why I will never wear one. Mustaches wear you. Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

Nvidia will investigate CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy
articles.description: In a memo to the company, Huang admitted that he had an affair.
articles.content: Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation. Nvidia also published a message that Huang sent to the company admitting that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed (though he didn’t mention her by name). A memo circulating among U.S. policymakers earlier this year claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang added that he’d “fallen short” of his responsibility to the company. “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said. As the AI race between the United States and China heats up, chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been a major focus. Huang also seems to have a close relationship with President Donald Trump, who’s been a cheerleader of the AI (or “superintelligence”) industry. In its announcement, Nvidia’s board said that it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or company secrets were compromised. It also said that Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” and that the board has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.” The investigation will be conducted by independent directors working with outside legal counsel. In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers. Other companies involved in the AI boom have warned employees to be wary of possible spies, including those offering sex or romance. articles.title: If Snap’s Specs are still ridiculously expensive, they’re also a lot more comfortable than they used to be
articles.description: Snap's Specs, which have been in development for many years now, are going to market this fall. Will they be a hit with users?
articles.content: When I tried a prototype of Snap’s Specs at CES in Las Vegas earlier this year, the experience left something to be desired. The company’s AR glasses — which the company calls a “new kind of computer” — were heavy (they weighed around 8 ounces) and fit rather uncomfortably on my face. The device was also hot, and made my face feel tingly — a common side-effect of smart glasses where massive computing is happening under the hood. Fast forward to late October, when I met back up with the Snap team at a Four Seasons in downtown San Francisco. By this time, the company had debuted Specs publicly during an event with CEO Evan Spiegel, and pre-orders of the company’s long-gestating headset were already underway. What I can say is this: Specs has improved the form factor significantly since my first brush with the device. The glasses now weigh nearly half of what the previous version did, slimming down to 132 grams, or approximately 4.6 ounces. They were quite comfortable and, during the hour-ish that I demo-ed the device, it did not heat up like the previous version had. Specs now comes in two sizes — 47mm and 52mm. The purpose here is purely to accommodate different head sizes, ensuring the glasses fit snugly on whoever’s face happens to be wearing them. They also now come equipped with spring hinges, which make the device more flexible and comfortable. However, if the body of the device has improved greatly, its soul is still a work-in-progress. The glasses can be fun — but they also still seem to lack a dedicated purpose, and one struggles to imagine how, specifically, this expensive head gear ($2,200 a pop) would prove useful in a daily capacity. When I asked Snap staff what the device was really for — fun and games or productivity — the answer was vague. The device attempts to be a bunch of things at once and, in the process, ends up feeling a little rudderless. I have racked my brain to come up with some daily use-cases for Specs. Some of the things I came up with were: By contrast, here are some of the areas I’m still not totally sold on as Specs use-cases: Specs is impressive for how the Snap team has managed to integrate a variety of user experiences into one unified device. There are a lot of impressive achievements here — specifically the spatial synching tech that allows two users to see the same thing simultaneously — that, with some further development, could be deployed towards some really interesting use cases. The bottom line is that Snap’s device can continue to grow and transform as the company iterates. It’s an interesting product that — like a lot of its peers — doesn’t necessarily seem to have a clear purpose but, in time, could become many things. What the device currently offers, however, may not be compelling enough to encourage people to shell out the cash that Snap is asking for. articles.title: Saudi Arabia turns to Syria for help as fighting with Houthis escalates
articles.content: DAMASCUS, Syria (AP) — Syria is preparing to send fighters to Saudi Arabia to deploy along its border and potentially help it fight Iranian-backed rebels in neighboring Yemen, three officials with knowledge of the plans told The Associated Press. Syrian military advisers have already deployed to Saudi Arabia, but no fighters have been sent to Yemen, according to a regional official and two Syrian officials, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly. Officials in Saudi Arabia did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Fighting escalated this summer in Yemen between the Houthi rebels and the government’s Saudi-backed forces. The Houthis have also launched direct and deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia in what is the latest front in the regional conflict that began in February when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran. Syria, which has a supply of battle-hardened fighters after a long civil war, has so far stayed on the sidelines. Saudi Arabia has an array of U.S.-supplied fighter jets and missile defenses but has been unable to defeat the Houthis in past rounds of conflict. While Saudi Arabia’s other allies have been reluctant to commit ground forces to its fight with the Houthis, the Syrian government is beholden to it. The Saudis provided funds to Syrian rebels during that country’s civil war and have promised much-needed financial assistance for Syria’s postwar reconstruction. A Syrian official said that an initial force of about 600 Syrian special forces fighters is expected to be deployed to Saudi Arabia in the coming week. The official said Saudi Arabia insisted the fighters be Syrian nationals, not foreigners who flocked to Syria during the civil war to join different rebel factions. The official said that a Syrian delegation led by Khaled Khattab, commander of the 82nd Division, had recently made a two-week visit to Saudi Arabia. A second Syrian official said 36 Syrian military officials visited a command and operations room in Jeddah staffed by Saudi and Yemeni officials and received briefings on the different front lines and areas of operation. A regional official with knowledge of the discussions said Syria had already deployed a “small number of advisers” to Saudi Arabia, where they helped train Yemeni forces inside the kingdom. An unnamed diplomatic official in Syria dismissed reports that Syrian forces were headed to Yemen, the country’s state-run news agency, SANA, reported on Saturday. The official said the agreement with Saudi Arabia focuses on training its military forces and building its capabilities. Syrian officials have said publicly that the country is discussing the possibility of joining a joint defense agreement recently signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed in August, commits the three countries to regard an attack against one as an attack on all three, and to deepen military cooperation in other ways. The two Syrian officials said that a decision had already been made — but not publicly announced — for Syria to join the Mecca pact, while the regional official said talks were still ongoing. One concern is that Syria might ask the other countries for their support against Israel, the regional official said. Following the ouster of Syria’s former President Bashar Assad in December 2024, Israeli forces seized control of a U.N.-patrolled buffer zone in southern Syria and have occupied it since. Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa says his government does not seek a conflict with Israel and has called for Israeli forces to withdraw. Syria and Saudi Arabia announced last week that they had signed a military cooperation agreement, without providing details. During a visit to Riyadh by al-Sharaa, the Saudi government agreed to lend Syria more than $400 million for postwar reconstruction of homes and basic infrastructure. Syria has turned down proposals by U.S. President Donald Trump for its forces to intervene against the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group in Lebanon. Al-Sharaa has said his focus is on rebuilding Syria after its lengthy civil war and that he wants to avoid getting embroiled in new conflicts. But Saudi Arabia has been key to its reintegration into the Arab world, which had largely shunned Syria under Assad’s rule. Syrian involvement in the fighting against the Houthis in Yemen could expose it to attacks by militias in neighboring Iraq that are allied with the Houthis. Magdy reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Abby Sewell in Beirut contributed to this report. He arrested a hacker, then spent 18 months clearing his own name. Now he’s a cybersecurity VC.
articles.description: Stephen Ward, a former Secret Service agent and Home Depot CISO, is preparing a second fund of roughly $250 million for Brightmind Partners.
articles.content: Every time venture capitalists write a check, they’re secretly running numbers in their heads about different exit scenarios. It’s their job as fiduciaries. But nearly all will tell you (publicly, anyway) that every portfolio company is headed for an IPO. Stephen Ward, the co-founder of Brightmind Partners, a two-year-old cybersecurity fund in New York, says otherwise outright. “You have to sell on the way up,” he says. Ward’s unvarnished pragmatism is one reason he stands out. Another is the size of his firm’s debut fund late last year: a whopping $250 million fund, which he closed with co-founder Gur Talpaz. A third reason is his résumé, which includes a stint with the Coast Guard, nine years in the Secret Service, and CISO jobs at TIAA and Home Depot before he ever thought about investing. One proof point that suggests the combination is working is SGNL, the identity security startup CrowdStrike agreed in January to buy for $740 million, 11 months after Brightmind led its Series A. Now Ward is raising a second fund, targeting roughly the same size as the first one. This time, though, he’ll be doing it without Talpaz, who left in April along with another early colleague, leaving Ward as the firm’s sole general partner. He’s betting on himself at a moment when early-stage cybersecurity startups are raising more money than later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade. His unemotional approach to exits traces back to an unlikely career. Ward says he grew up in northwest New Jersey between two farms, in a family that couldn’t afford college for his older brothers. After high school, he joined the Coast Guard, inspired by a commercial of a man jumping out of a helicopter, though he says he barely knew how to swim at the time. He spent four years in search and rescue. Afterward, he studied criminal justice at Seton Hall in New Jersey and thought half-heartedly about law school. “I didn’t know what I wanted to do,” Ward told me last week over Zoom, wearing a pale hooded sweatshirt and looking more like a basketball coach than a venture capitalist. “I was kind of lost. I missed the military and the camaraderie and all of that.” After graduating in 1998, he says, he mailed out some 300 résumés but no one responded. A Seton Hall professor who was also a chaplain to Secret Service personnel, as well as to members of the FBI and CIA, began introducing him around, and the Secret Service called first. The Secret Service has two primary missions: protecting people and investigating financial crimes. Ward gravitated to investigations, then to “cyber” after the September 11 attacks in 2001. That year, he married a former college classmate, an American-born Syrian Muslim. Colleagues warned him the background check would be “miserable.” (They’re still happily married.) What came next took Ward’s life down an unexpected path. Stationed in New York, he arrested a hacker who’d pulled off the largest credit card data theft of that era. Instead of charging him, however, Ward flipped him, turning him into an informant and running him for about three years. But the hacker kept hacking behind Ward’s back, and after he was caught again, he told the agency, as a diversionary tactic, that Ward was in on it. By that time, Ward had left for the private sector, and he ultimately spent roughly 18 months clearing his name. “It was hard to get out of bed,” he said of that period, describing the investigation as “almost like a spouse cheating on you,” given his love of the agency. The hacker ultimately received a 20-year sentence, and Audible bought the rights to the story, turning it into an eight-episode podcast called “Operation Firewall.” Ward’s corporate career has been a success by most measures, though he describes it as a series of jumps he really wasn’t qualified to make. His first private-sector job at J.P. Morgan, where he was recruited in 2007 to build a cybersecurity unit, was the hardest transition of his career, he says. He felt like “the dumbest person in the room,” missed his Secret Service crew, and twice thought about going back, unaware he was still under investigation. He stuck it out and now calls the investment bank the “best management school.” Six years as CISO at the financial services company TIAA followed, and then two years at Home Depot starting in 2019. But in 2021, feeling burned out, he quit without anything lined up for the first time since age 16. That chapter didn’t last long. The founders of Wiz, whose security software Ward had used at Home Depot, put him on a short list for a job at their company. Jeff Horing, a venture capitalist at Insight Partners, which had co-led Wiz’s $100 million Series A round in late 2020, interviewed Ward for the role, then offered him one at Insight instead. It’s a good-news, bad-news story, given that Wiz was acquired last year by Google for $32 billion. When I asked him about it last week, Ward observed that the friend who took the Wiz job “made life-changing money,” but said it doesn’t bother him. Regardless, he spent just three years at Insight, where he says he worked on Wiz, Abnormal Security, and Elisity, which IonQ agreed in October to buy for up to $1.3 billion. Then, at age 49, he thought about striking out on his own for the first time. He says people told him it was a young man’s game. He left anyway and began cold-emailing limited partners. Ultimately, fewer than 20 LPs filled the fund, including Horing. Ward started Brightmind in 2024 with Talpaz, a CrowdStrike corporate development executive whose deals overlapped with Ward’s during his time at Insight. Tayler Sipperly, another CrowdStrike corporate development alum, was the firm’s third employee. The partnership ended this past spring. Asked what happened, Ward, using carefully worded legalese, cited “differences in opinions regarding operations and the future of Brightmind.” In August, Talpaz and Sipperly co-founded a new venture firm with Elia Zaitsev, CrowdStrike’s global CTO for the past three years. Called Cognition, it’s now reportedly targeting a $170 million first fund to back cybersecurity startups. Sipperly says that he and Talpaz “continue to support the existing Brightmind portfolio companies as well as its limited partners” and that they “remain on the board of a number of the Brightmind portfolio companies.” Brightmind’s first fund has made 14 investments to date, with one exit: that SNGL sale. Some investors asked why Brightmind didn’t ride out that bet even longer. But Ward says he’s seen enough across his career that he feels confident in warning founders when they’re “going to race past the turn.” In cybersecurity, he says, the best sales come between a startup’s third and seventh years. Indeed, he says his team tracks every security acquisition and what buyers are building versus buying. If Palo Alto Networks is likely to buy something, he says, CrowdStrike will experience “FOMO, then Zscaler is going to look over and go, ‘What did they just do? I should probably do the same thing.’” Understanding how the pieces fit together is the trick, Ward explained, offering some hypotheticals. If CrowdStrike is building a product, he said, it’s unlikely to buy a portfolio company that makes something similar. Palo Alto Networks might love a company, but not if buying it would force its customers to switch away from something it bought five years ago. “It’s very easy to go, ‘Good match,’ ‘terrible match,’” he said. “And that’s really what we spend a ton of time figuring out.” He has timing on his side, at least. Early-stage cybersecurity startups are outraising their later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade, according to PitchBook, which counts $4.7 billion worth of seed-through-Series B deals through September. That total is already ahead of the entirety of 2025, even though the number of deals fell to 248 from 358 last year. Seed rounds in particular are ballooning, per PitchBook. The average cybersecurity seed round jumped to $8.4 million in the first nine months of this year, from $5.54 million a year earlier. Ward questions how much of that money is really going to AI security. By PitchBook’s count, 278 deals in the first half of 2026 were bucketed as such, but his team’s manual review found only 30 true ones. He doesn’t think Anthropic or OpenAI will “take over the security world,” but instead will do “just enough.” For real-time protection, which he terms “zero second,” he favors cyber-specific models that run locally on a customer’s own systems, like that of Empirical Security. He also looks for startups that could trounce established companies that he considers vulnerable, name-checking 27-year-old Qualys and 24-year-old Tenable. Ward says Brightmind’s second fund won’t be entirely cybersecurity, focusing about 20% on AI infrastructure deals. He expects a meaningful number of teams to come from Israel, too. (Roughly 40% of the debut fund’s startups are based in Tel Aviv.) Asked about the founders he’s most comfortable backing, the response is immediate: second-time founders who stick together. Brightmind is comprised of five people right now: COO Iva Messy, also a Seton Hall graduate, came from venture firms Felicis and Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) on the recommendation of Ward’s cousin, Carl Eschenbach, a former Workday CEO who is now back at Sequoia. Sven Wollschlaeger, a Midwesterner whom Ward calls one of the hardest-working people he’s known, spent three years alongside Ward at Insight and is a principal at Brightmind. CTO Jamie Mneimneh, whom Ward first hired at Home Depot as a distinguished engineer, is the most technical person of the team. He built the cloud computing environment on AWS where the firm tests startups’ products. Mneimneh also built the AI agents that now source most of Brightmind’s deal flow, which is how the firm avoids hiring a bench of analysts and keeps management fees down, says Ward. Taylor Cleveland, Ward’s chief of staff at Home Depot, joined the firm a few months ago. For all the career changes, Ward says the real force driving him hasn’t changed. He grew up without money and still worries it could happen again, saying he’s being paid to produce a “3x net fund,” and he’s “not going to celebrate until we get that.” Said Ward: “I don’t know what’s wrong with me. I have a level of being very naive to like, not being qualified to do something. I’ve just always looked at people and been like, ‘Okay, you know more than me today, but tomorrow, it’s going to be a little less, and the day after that, it’s going to be less, and eventually, I’m going to catch you and surpass you, and I’m going to know more than you.’ That’s how competitive I am.” Update: Comments from Sipperly were added after publication. articles.content: Suno is facing yet another pair of lawsuits. A group of rights holders of Elvis Presley’s music and the publisher of some of Eminem‘s biggest records are suing the AI music company, claiming it illegally generates music and lyrics that mimic those artists. The lawyers in the Presley suit claim that Suno has violated Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security (ELVIS) Act, which makes it illegal for an AI company to clone a singer’s voice. In the suit, lawyers representing Presley’s rights holders argue that “Suno has mechanically encoded itself with artists’ identities, hard-work, creativity, and time, and harnessed them all for a consistent conveyor belt of cold hard cash.“ These suits closely mirror one filed by Jason Isbell and others in September, which claimed Suno created imitations of the plaintiffs but did not claim copyright infringement directly. Later in the complaint, the lawyers write that “Suno’s ravenous race to the bottom aims to make human creativity obsolete, coldly replicating without a license in seconds what takes years to learn, struggle with, maintain, and endlessly attempt to make better and perfect.” Suno spokesperson Cat McCormack told The Verge that, “Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone’s name or likeness, and we prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist’s work. To protect against this, we do not allow prompts for specific artists’ names and songs and work with third-party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse. We are always working to strengthen our guardrails and we will continue to add new safeguards that protect artists and our users.” This adds to the pile of lawsuits Suno is currently facing from Sony, UMG, Isbell, Reservoir Media, and more.

articles.title: Russia targets emergency crews at the site of a deadly strike in southern Ukraine
articles.content: ZAPORIZHZHIA, Ukraine (AP) — A Russian drone struck emergency workers on rescue missions in southern Ukraine on Sunday, hitting a former school and nearby shelter that had been earlier blasted by multiple Russian guided bombs as residents waited for humanitarian aid, authorities said. No one was injured in Sunday’s strike on the village of Komyshuvakha, but specialized rescue equipment was damaged, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service. Ukraine said Monday’s attack on the same location killed at least 55 people, near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region. As of Sunday afternoon, 45 people were listed as missing, according to the acting head of the regional military administration, Mykhailo Semikin. Many of the bodies recovered have not been identified and DNA analysis is ongoing. Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, told The Associated Press on Saturday that he was still looking for his wife, but had heard no word from rescuers. “She went to get humanitarian aid, and a 3-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?” he said. “She didn’t come home, and they didn’t find her body there. She isn’t in the morgue, and she isn’t here alive.” Ukraine has routinely accused Russia of conducting multiple strikes at the same site in quick succession to target emergency crews responding to the initial attack. On Saturday, police officers and relatives gathered in Zaporizhzhia for a farewell ceremony for six officers killed in Russian strikes on Komyshuvakha, including four who died near the former school. Rain fell as families wept beside the coffins, and officers held portraits of their fallen colleagues. “They used every skill at their disposal to protect themselves. But when the enemy deliberately gathered civilians in one place and then launched strikes against them, no skills could have helped,” said Andrii Khomenko, a police lieutenant colonel who had worked alongside the victims. The community also said goodbye to three residents among the dead. Among those mourning was Yurii Karapetian, whose wife Natalia was killed. He said she was distributing bread to those in the shelter when the Russian bombs struck. “This pain, I would say, is unbearable,” he said, and urged the international community to act. “The whole world must understand that if (the Russians) are not stopped, they will not stop. They will not stop at Ukraine. They will not stop anywhere,” he said. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday called the attack on emergency crews in Komyshuvakha “absolute cynicism and brutality” in a post on X. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Sunday that France and other European representatives would participate in the U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11. “France will be there and will ensure that Europe’s voice is heard,” Barrot told RTL radio. He did not specify who would represent France, or whether European officials would participate directly in negotiations. The talks were previously presented as a trilateral meeting between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv, with U.S. President Donald Trump predicting a “very big” deal with Russia extending beyond Ukraine to “all of Europe”. This raised concerns that European countries might be sidelined in negotiations over their own security. Russian strikes in Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk region have left more than 600,000 people without power, Zelenskyy wrote on X on Sunday. Russia’s defense ministry claimed its forces had struck an electrical substation that powered Ukrainian “military-industrial enterprises”. Other regions in Ukraine also faced outages. Russia launched 115 missiles, 1,900 guided aerial bombs and more than 3,000 drones against Ukraine in the past week, Zelenskyy said on X. Many of the missiles had been produced this year, he added, calling on Ukraine’s partners to sanction entities involved in their production. “If the world does not have enough anti-ballistic capabilities to protect Ukrainian skies, then the missiles must be stopped on the production lines,” he said. The Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, the largest in Europe, has lost its external power supply after a damaged power line was disconnected for safety, the plant’s management reported Sunday. It said the plant was powered by backup diesel generators since an automatic protection system shut down the damaged Ferosplavna line. Ukraine’s state nuclear operator, Energoatom, also reported on Sunday that the plant was relying on generators. The plant went offline soon after being captured by Russia early in the war, but needs power to keep essential cooling systems running. Its external power supply has periodically been severed, raising fears of a nuclear accident in case of protracted outages, as Moscow and Kyiv blamed each other for strikes that damaged nearby power lines. Russia launched 164 drones across Ukraine overnight into Sunday, 137 of which were shot down, the Ukrainian Air Force said that morning. Hours later, one person was killed and three others injured as Russian forces struck a residential neighbourhood in Dnipro, according to local administration head Oleksandr Hanzha. Russia’s defense ministry said Sunday that its forces destroyed 142 Ukrainian drones during the night — including over Russia, Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine and the Azov Sea. This story corrects the number of police officers killed in the strike on the former school. AP writer Thomas Adamson contributed from Paris. Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

A Michigan utility’s iffy plan to trap CO2 from its new gas plants
articles.description: This story was originally published by Canary Media. Can a utility commit to building massive gas plants and still achieve zero carbon emissions? DTE Electric in southeast Michigan says yes, and it outlines how in a 20-year plan currently being considered by regulators. The key, the utility says, will be carbon capture and sequestration — collecting carbon […]
articles.content: DTE Monroe power plant (Photo by Susan J. Demas/Michigan Advance)This story was originally published by Canary Media. Can a utility commit to building massive gas plants and still achieve zero carbon emissions? DTE Electric in southeast Michigan says yes, and it outlines how in a 20-year plan currently being considered by regulators. The key, the utility says, will be carbon capture and sequestration — collecting carbon dioxide emissions from two proposed gas-fired power plants and storing them underground. Michigan state law says power generation must be carbon-free by 2040. The gas plants would go online in 2031 and 2032, and carbon capture equipment would be added by 2035, according to the long-range integrated resource plan that DTE filed with the state public service commission in September. The problem, as critics see it, is that carbon capture and sequestration has not been successfully deployed by electric utilities in the U.S. thus far. Even if the technology becomes economically viable, public opposition to the technology is likely to remain strong, as evidenced by the response to the Michigan Legislature’s efforts to adopt a carbon sequestration law. Public outcry has also erupted in neighboring states over plans for carbon dioxide pipelines and injection wells. In other words, DTE proposes to invest billions of customers’ dollars in gas plants that are dependent on a nascent and uncertain solution to comply with state law on emissions that would harm the climate and public health. Utilities across the country are grappling with the same predicament of needing to meet steep increases in energy demand driven by data centers while also transitioning to clean energy. DTE’s plan calls for closing the half-century-old, 3-gigawatt Monroe coal plant and building 15 GW of renewables — mostly solar — and 4.5 gigawatts of energy storage. The utility also proposes two new gas-fired plants totaling 2.1 GW in the Detroit area, one of them in the same county as the coal plant. That’s more than double the amount of gas-fired generation DTE proposed to add in the long-range plan it filed four years ago. At that time, it said 946 megawatts of gas-fired generation with carbon capture could fill the gap left by the coal plant closure. While DTE has framed the gas plants as simply replacing the retiring coal plant, clean energy advocates believe that the expanded plan is meant to accommodate upcoming data centers. DTE has signed contracts with Oracle and Google for a combined 2.4 gigawatts’ worth of power, and its proposal cites ​“2.4 GW of new customer load” as among the changes since the 2022 plan was filed. “Just looking at the numbers, it’s hard not to draw that direct link,” said Helen Li, senior attorney with the nonprofit law firm Earthjustice, which represented environmentalists in regulatory proceedings over the planned Google data center. “DTE is trying to lock in billions of dollars of new gas plants now on the promise that later they will seek to spend billions more to try to bring those plants into compliance with Michigan laws. Both of those issues should be fully evaluated now before DTE is allowed to start spending ratepayer money locking in new fossil generation.” Over the coming year, state regulators will study and decide whether to approve DTE’s proposal. A DTE spokesperson declined to comment and referred Canary Media to the company’s website. Costs and doubts Michigan first passed a clean energy law in 2008, and a 2023 update laid out what types of energy can be used to meet the requirement that the state’s utilities generate 80% of their power from clean sources by 2035 and 100% by 2040. Sixty percent of generation must come from renewables by 2035. The law says gas plants can comply for the nonrenewable but ​“clean” portion of generation if they capture at least 90% of emissions from their smokestacks. Whether that will happen is highly debatable. The financial and industry analytics firm S&P Global notes in a report that carbon capture and sequestration ​“is a mature and scalable technology for decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors. However, despite over 50 years of operations, CCS remains at early stages of deployment.” The report cites cost, financial risk, market uncertainty, and the complexity of constructing and monitoring the infrastructure as reasons that the technology is used in only a small number of sites worldwide. Most of those are related to enhanced oil recovery, in which the carbon dioxide is used to push oil out of waning reservoirs, providing an additional revenue stream. The one commercial power plant in the U.S. to use carbon capture — the Petra Nova project at a Texas coal plant — has had a rocky history, including a three-year shutdown and missed targets. The Environmental Protection Agency last year reported that ​“it is extremely unlikely that the extensive infrastructure for CCS can be deployed” by the 2032 compliance date set under the Biden rule,” as E&E News noted. Carbon capture equipment on power plants is expensive in part because it takes a considerable amount of electricity to operate, and that electricity must be clean if the goal is zero emissions. DTE estimates it will take $6.4 billion to build the two new gas plants. The cost of carbon capture and sequestration is hard to predict, so the plants’ price tag could balloon higher. “It’s incredibly expensive,” said Charlotte Jameson, chief policy officer of the Michigan Environmental Council, which has intervened in the regulatory process for DTE’s long-range plan. “When we’re talking about carbon capture and sequestration, we’re not just talking about the actual capture technology on the smokestack, which is expensive in and of itself, but also building out infrastructure to pipe the carbon dioxide to a place where it can be sequestered. I think it would be really easy at this juncture to undervalue what it would cost. That’s a huge, risky bet for ratepayers and Michigan as a whole.” In recent months, regulators have been hashing out how much data centers will pay to help build the generation they need. While these proceedings are separate from DTE’s long-range plan, advocates see them as related — and worry that residents will wind up shouldering too much financial burden. On October 30, the Michigan attorney general requested that the public service commission reexamine DTE’s contract with Google to power its planned data center, citing the risk that ratepayers will be charged unfairly. Clean energy implications While some advocates would prefer not to see new data centers at all, they argue that if the facilities must be built, their need for electricity could be met without increasing emissions or relying on carbon capture. “We are looking to ensure that DTE is maximizing the full suite of clean technologies — renewables, storage, demand response, transmission, et cetera,” Earthjustice’s Li said, ​“rather than defaulting to more fossil generation, for meeting the needs of its ratepayers and serving AI new data center load.” Nationwide, experts and regulators have indeed called on data centers to be flexible with the amount of power they use at a given time, so utilities don’t have to build extra capacity to meet periods of peak demand. The Michigan Environmental Council’s Jameson is worried that the state’s clean energy law won’t force DTE to ensure that the gas plants capture their emissions. The law allows for multiple extensions to the deadlines for reasons including grid reliability, feasibility of installing renewables, and other factors. “Those off-ramps are written pretty broadly,” Jameson said, noting that they were adopted before the data center boom. ​“So if data center load makes it too difficult to meet renewable energy standards, there is a lot of risk we just blow through our renewable energy standards and clean energy targets and those become effectively meaningless.” Mark Templeton, director of the Abrams Environmental Law Clinic at the University of Chicago, has represented community groups in other proceedings involving DTE. He noted that the utility’s 2022 long-range plan ​“was critically important in establishing the schedule for closing significant coal-fired power generation.” “This is equally important in terms of figuring out what the replacement is,” he said. ​“Locking in continued use of gas is better than coal, but that’s not saying much.”

Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
articles.description: Tuning in to electronic noise can tell us whether electrons have paired up or not.
articles.content: Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why. In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate. The missing electrons Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said.Read full article Comments

Progress on the ESPEN NTD Portal in 2026: country data, open methods and decision tools
articles.content: The ESPEN NTD Portal home page (version 4.0, relaunched in May 2025). © WHO AFRO / ESPEN Brazzaville, Congo, 8 November 2026 — The ESPEN NTD Portal is the open-access data platform for the five neglected tropical diseases targeted by preventive chemotherapy in the WHO African Region. Its progress in 2026 and priorities for 2027 were presented to ESPEN's Regional Programme Advisory Group and Steering Committee in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in late October. Annual reports from national programmes, submitted through the WHO Joint Application Package (JAP), are now published country by country once validated. Between June and October 2026, endemicity and treatment data for 2025 were released for 33 programmes, and nine more countries confirmed no mass drug administration in 2025. National programmes with 2025 endemicity and treatment data on the Portal, by release date. Source: ESPEN NTD Portal, Data updates. © WHO AFRO / ESPEN In October, ESPEN published how it processes these data: nine standard operating procedures, with the full protocol in English, French and Portuguese. ESPEN harmonizes country reports but does not verify field data, so figures may differ from those in WHO global databases. Since January 2026, 44 national programmes have had a Country Health Information Platform (CHIP) dashboard of their current and historical data. New surveys in ESPEN Collect, the free mobile survey tool, have been hosted on WHO Regional Office for Africa servers since 1 October 2026, and more than 2.5 million earlier records have been transferred. The JAP Upload Tool is also hosted on WHO servers. An independent evaluation of the ESPEN Geospatial Microplanner found that, in three Sightsavers-supported pilot areas in Guinea-Bissau, Liberia and Nigeria, 61,930 more people were treated in 2025 than in 2024, and 463 priority settlements were reached for the first time. Monthly questions to the ESPEN GenAI Assistant, developed with Dimagi, rose from 49 to 295 between August 2025 and August 2026. Engaged Portal sessions (visits with active use) rose by 5% to 28,311 in the 12 months to August 2026; since January 2023, 46.7% have come from countries of the WHO African Region. Priorities for 2027 include consolidating the Portal's tools on one WHO-hosted platform, bringing ESPEN Collect fully under WHO management, piloting online reporting linked to national DHIS2 health information systems, digitizing schistosomiasis community data workbooks and extending the Geospatial Microplanner to nine countries. Renewed data-sharing agreements, sent to 48 country programmes in February 2026, let each ministry of health decide, once signed, which of its data are published on the Portal. ESPEN thanks national programmes and partners for their contributions.

Every Minnesota House district voted more blue than in 2024, leading to a DFL trifecta in the state government. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer) Stories From The States is a weekly podcast from States Newsroom that explores, through personal stories, how people and communities across America are being affected by government decisions. Listen now wherever you get your podcasts. An enormous blue wave crashed over all levels of government this midterm cycle. Congressional seats, governor’s mansions and state legislatures flipped from Republican to Democrat, some in surprising fashion. Democrats claimed “trifecta” power in some state capitals, broke supermajorities in others and won other influential statewide offices. For months, the Trump administration tried to assert federal control over the election process to bolster Republicans’ chances of maintaining power. President Donald Trump pushed GOP-led states to gerrymander their congressional districts, demanded state voter rolls through legal challenges and threatened to send armed federal agents to the polls. Despite fears about possible interference or intimidation heading into Election Day, voters turned out en masse and have shifted the course of policymaking over the next several years in their states and on Capitol Hill. In Episode 53, we’re reflecting on the state of American democracy, election integrity and what Tuesday’s results could mean for policymaking in reshaped statehouses. States Newsroom democracy reporter Jonathan Shorman and Evening Wrap newsletter writer Danielle Gaines will chat about the major trends from this election, what surprised them and what could be next. articles.title: Consumers Energy gets more time to negotiate with dam sale opponents, but they don't seem interested
articles.description: Consumers Energy has received a second extension of the deadline for Michigan regulators to issue a final decision on its proposed hydroelectric dam sale to an out-of-state private equity firm.
articles.content: Shoreline of the Hodenpyl Dam. (Courtesy of Consumers Energy.)Consumers Energy will get more time to reach a settlement with opponents of its plan to sell its 13 hydroelectric dams.The Michigan Public Service Commission has agreed to Consumers Energy's request for a second waiver of the agency’s statutory deadline to issue a decision in the utility’s proposed dams sale.That gives the utility more time to negotiate with intervenors in the case that oppose the sale. But it's unclear who Consumers Energy is negotiating with, after most intervenors left the first round of negotiations still opposed."The attorney general, the governor's office, the Michigan Department of Natural Resources, the conservation groups, the industrial customers, have all said the negotiations are not going anywhere," said Howard Learner with the Environmental Law and Policy Center, which represents one of the intervenors.Consumers Energy has proposed to sell its 13 aging hydroelectric dams along the Au Sable, Grand, Kalamazoo, Manistee and Muskegon rivers to Confluence Hydro, a private equity energy company, for $1 each. Consumers would then purchase the power generated by the dams, and the new owner would be financially responsible to ensure the safety of the dams.In June, an administrative law judge found that the proposal was too risky and not in the public interest.Learner said the Michigan Public Service Commission should do its job and make a final decision based on the findings of the administrative law judge. "Enough is enough. The proposed dam sale is a bad deal for ratepayers, for the rivers and for safe dams in Michigan. This is a bad deal that should be rejected by the public service commission. Let's move forward," Learner said.Learner said the disposition of the dams should be made on a case-by-case basis, since each one is different and affects different groups of people. Consumers Energy continues to insist that a settlement is possible.“We understand the desire for communities and our coworkers for an outcome in this case. We are providing for a little more time to reach a constructive agreement that will be a win for our customers, Michigan, and the communities we care about,” said Chris Fultz, Consumers Energy’s senior vice president of electric supply, in a statement.“We continue to work with others to find solutions to ensure these dams will continue to operate safely and responsibly for years to come," Fultz said."We recognize some parties have publicly opposed continuing settlement efforts. Consumers Energy respectfully disagrees and remains committed to working in good faith to achieve a constructive settlement for the benefit of customers, communities and the State of Michigan.” The commission said it was reasonable to allow negotiations to continue, but warned that this will be the final extension granted in this case to Consumers, and any settlement agreement reached in the matter must be filed by 5 p.m. on December 9. If no settlement is filed by the December 9 deadline, the Commission will issue a final order on the sale on December 17.Learner said it's not unheard of for the agency to decide a case differently than an administrative law judge. But he said the judge in this case wrote an unusually detailed, 312-page opinion based on an extensive evidentiary record."The commission would really have to look at the same evidence, the same evidentiary record, and have a factual basis as well as a legal basis for reaching a different conclusion," Learner said. "And in this particular case, I think that would just be very, very hard for the commission to do in a legally sustainable way."

articles.title: Black Michiganders helped push Abdul El‑Sayed to victory – but he was less popular with this key voting bloc than some other Democrats
articles.description: Early election results do not indicate whether Black voters embraced El-Sayed’s progressive platform or simply voted for the Democratic candidate.
articles.content: This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article. This story was first published in The Conversation Progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race was one of the most-watched contests in the 2026 midterm elections. As the results for this race came in, I had my eye on one demographic: Black voters. I am a political scientist who studies Black political behavior. My research has been published in numerous journals, as well as in my forthcoming book, “Black Resilience,” which examines Black voters’ political participation. Wayne County voters The support of Black voters for El-Sayed was not a given. In the August primary, 62% of Detroit voters chose U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens over El-Sayed. Many pundits predicted it would be difficult for El-Sayed to gain support in Detroit, which is about 75% Black. After the primary, El-Sayed made overtures by sharing his plans to improve the lives of Black Americans, which included supporting the growth of minority-owned businesses, creating more affordable housing, eliminating food deserts and expanding the Rx Kids cash assistance program nationwide. About 91.8% of Detroit voters supported El-Sayed in the general election, according to the city’s unofficial results. Detroit City Clerk Janice Winfrey said 209,924 residents voted in the 2026 midterms, up about 21% from the 2022 midterm elections. For the 2024 presidential election, 247,770 city residents cast a ballot. In fact, El-Sayed received 70.6% of Wayne County votes, which includes Detroit. In 2024, Kamala Harris received 62.7% of the vote in Wayne County. Statewide support is holding steady In the 2024 presidential election, Michigan’s Democratic vote share fell to 48.3%, from 50.6% in 2020, as the state went for Donald Trump instead of Democratic nominee Harris. Despite their ideological differences, Sen. Elissa Slotkin and El-Sayed drew similar support among Black voters. In 2024, Slotkin – a moderate Democrat – won 48.6% of the vote, a small margin over Mike Rogers, who was the Republican candidate in that race. In 2026, El-Sayed defeated Rogers statewide by a substantially wider margin, winning 52% of the vote. In other words, these early election results do not indicate whether Black voters embraced El-Sayed’s progressive platform or simply voted for the Democratic candidate. Voters may have been rejecting Republican Party politics or expressing anger toward Trump over pocketbook issues. Researchers from Michigan State University found that precincts with more than 80% of Black voters supported Democratic statewide candidates over Republicans at a rate of 92% to 94% during the 2024 general election, which is only slightly lower than the 94% to 95% levels observed in similar precincts during the 2020 contest between Trump and Joe Biden. Even while Black voters overwhelmingly support Democrats, small shifts in their support and turnout can influence the outcome of close and competitive races. These shifts may help explain differing outcomes, including El-Sayed’s victory in 2026 and Harris’ defeat there in 2024. While Black voter support for El-Sayed was high, estimated at around 86% statewide, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s support among Black voters was about 94% in the 2022 gubernatorial race, according to an ABC exit poll. Similarly, preelection polling indicated that Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, polled more favorably among nonwhite voters compared to El-Sayed. NBC exit poll data shows that 86% of Black voters in Michigan supported El-Sayed, while 90% supported Benson, who won the governorship over Republican John James. Historic power and unity Black voters are often strategic voters who support the candidate they believe best aligns with Black interests, which has usually been the Democratic candidate since the Civil Rights Movement. Generally, Black voters have made their electoral choices based on what’s believed to be best for the group as a whole – a concept described by political scientist Michael C. Dawson as linked fate. However, recent research shows that Black social networks and institutions, including churches and civic organizations, reinforce expectations of political solidarity. Weaker ties to these networks may lessen the social pressure that encourages Black Americans to participate in politics and support Democratic candidates. Lower participation by Black Americans could lead to elected officials paying less attention to issues important to Black voters, such as affordability and the cost of living, healthcare, and reducing racial discrimination. If officials assume Black voters will remain loyal to Democrats, they’re under less pressure to win their votes by addressing their concerns. My research has demonstrated that after the 2024 election, Black women in particular felt frustrated with the Democratic Party, yet they participated in elections despite these frustrations. An agenda that matters El-Sayed was part of a field of notable Democratic candidates in this election cycle. For example, Angie Nixon, a state representative in Florida, championed affordability alongside a moratorium on evictions and a universal jobs program, while James Talarico, a former schoolteacher in Texas, focused on public education. El-Sayed is a former public health official who had not previously held elected office. This may have turned off some Black voters who often value governing experience. El-Sayed advocated for Medicare For All and lowering the costs of gas prices and groceries. Although he doesn’t identify as a democratic socialist, El-Sayed campaigned with several progressive elected officials, such as U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders endorsed El-Sayed on the day he announced his candidacy in 2025. El-Sayed also campaigned with the Black establishment, including U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. Former President Barack Obama spoke at a rally for El-Sayed in Detroit in October 2026. Stevens, who lost the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed in the primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers after she attended a service with the Republican candidate at a predominantly Black church in Detroit two days before the election. Stevens’ tactic drew severe backlash from Democratic leaders and may have mobilized some Black voters to turn out for El-Sayed on Election Day. “I felt like she pimped my community,” one Black voter from Detroit told ABC News in response to Stevens’ last-minute endorsement of Rogers. Christine Slaughter, Assistant Professor of Political Science, Boston University

articles.description: Strong earthquake shakes central Japan, shattering store windows and injuring at least 22 AP News M5.7 quake strikes central Japan; over 20 injured Japan Today Magnitude 5.9 earthquake strikes off eastern Japan, shakes Tokyo Anadolu Ajansı A strong earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 5.7 strikes Japan, meteorological agency says ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos Magnitude 5.7 quake injures dozen
articles.content: TOKYO (AP) — A strong earthquake shook central Japan early Sunday, shattering store windows, causing people to flee buildings and leaving at least 22 people injured, according to local media. Japan’s Meteorological Agency put the quake’s magnitude at 5.7, while the U.S. Geological Survey reported it at magnitude 5.5. Smaller aftershocks were reported. A wide area near Aichi Prefecture was affected, including the city of Hamamatsu, the ancient capitals of Kyoto and Nara and nearby prefectures of Yamanashi, where Mount Fuji is located, as well as Gifu. Japanese TV footage showed shattered store windows and scattered shards of glass on the streets. A bookstore was left with mounds of books that had flown off the shelves. The injuries included people who fell from stairs while they were trying to flee. The quake, which struck at 1:04 a.m., was located about 40 kilometers (25 miles) below the earth’s surface in Shizuoka Prefecture. Aichi and Shizuoka are neighboring regions. They are far enough from Tokyo that the quake was not felt there. The most violent shaking was felt in Aichi, according to official seismic assessments. The meteorological agency warned people to brace for possible strong quakes in the coming week, especially the next two to three days. “Please be on the lookout for mudslides, falling rocks and the possible effects from rainfall,” Ayataka Ebita, an agency official, told reporters. He said no apparent change was detected so far to the Nankai Trough plate, where scientists say a megaquake can possibly hit. The Shinkansen bullet trains were running at slower speeds in the affected areas as a precautionary measure. Sometimes quakes can damage the railways the trains run on. Japan is located in an area that is prone to earthquakes. Authorities frequently instruct people to stock up on bottled water, food and batteries, have plans ready to hide under tables and keep comfortable walking shoes at hand. Lions put LB Jack Campbell on IR, less than a week after he was hospitalized with neck injury
articles.content: ALLEN PARK, Mich. (AP) — Detroit Lions All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell has been placed on injured reserve, less than a week after he was hospitalized with a neck injury. The Lions made the move Saturday along with adding Nick Whiteside to the active roster from the practice squad and promoting edge rusher Anthony Lucas and running back Jabari Small from the practice squad. Detroit (5-2) plays at Miami (1-6) on Sunday. Campbell said earlier in the week that he has full movement in his lower body and is continuing to make progress with movement in his upper body. “I know there’s still work ahead, but I remain very optimistic,” Campbell said Wednesday in a statement released by the team. Campbell was injured early in the fourth quarter of a win over Minnesota last Sunday. He was face down on the turf and not moving after hitting Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson. Campbell was evaluated by medical personnel before being strapped to a board and carefully lifted onto the cart. “Jack continues to improve, which is all great news,” coach Dan Campbell said on Friday.
